title: Choices and Effects
short: Name a choice (a story, a contrast, a repetition), then explain its effect on the audience and how it serves the purpose.
trouble: Learners list devices (feature spotting) without saying why they matter.

blocks.html: The heart of rhetorical analysis is a two-part move: name a choice, then explain its effect on the audience and how it serves the purpose.

Choice → effect → purpose. “By [choice], the writer [effect on the audience], which [serves the purpose].” A choice can be a word, a sentence pattern, an example, an order, an appeal, or what the writer leaves out.

Every writer chooses among many ways to say a thing. Asking why this way, and not another, is how analysis finds meaning. A good test is to imagine the plain version: if Lincoln had said “We can’t really dedicate this ground,” what would be lost?

head: Choice
Effect on the audience
How it serves the purpose
rows: Lincoln: “we can not dedicate—we can not consecrate—we can not hallow—this ground”
each verb is holier than the last, so the confession of weakness builds instead of shrinking
turns the duty from the speakers to the listeners: honor the dead by finishing their work
Lincoln, Second Inaugural: “And the war came.”
a four-word sentence after long ones lands like a blow
presents the war as something both sides failed to prevent, inviting reconciliation
“your,” not “our,” sets him apart from the holiday
makes listeners feel the gap between their celebration and the lives of the enslaved
blocks.cap: Choices, their effects, and the purposes they serve.

blocks.html: Strong analysis uses precise verbs: emphasizes, contrasts, invites, reassures, unsettles, shames, honors, builds, undercuts, echoes, narrows, broadens, anticipates. Weak analysis leans on shows and uses.

blocks.title: From spotting to analyzing
blocks.q: A student writes: “Lincoln uses repetition.” Make it analysis.
steps: Name the specific choice: “we can not” three times, with verbs that rise from dedicate to consecrate to hallow.
Say the effect: the listeners hear the speakers admit, more strongly each time, that their words fall short.
Tie it to purpose: if words can’t honor the dead, only deeds can; so the living must finish the work.
blocks.a: “Lincoln repeats ‘we can not,’ each time with a holier verb, to admit that words fall short of the soldiers’ sacrifice, so that honoring them becomes a task for the living rather than a ceremony.”

blocks.html: Listing devices without saying why they matter, sometimes called feature spotting. “He uses repetition, imagery and a rhetorical question” tells the reader nothing about the speech. Check: every device you name should be followed by “which …” or “so that …” and an effect on the audience.

cards.text: Douglass asks what the Fourth of July means to a slave, forcing a celebrating audience to look at the holiday through other eyes.
Lincoln’s four-word sentence “And the war came.” makes the war seem to arrive on its own, as something no one fully chose, which prepares listeners for “malice toward none.”
